Artificial turf repair in Kissimmee, Florida

Artificial turf repair fixes the specific thing that failed, not the whole lawn: a wrinkle, an open seam, a lifted edge, a burn spot from window glare, or a low area that holds water after a Kissimmee storm. Most single-issue repairs are a half-day visit. Published national ranges run roughly $350 to $2,400 depending on scope; a firm number follows photos or a site visit.

Reviewed by Luis Austin, owner · Last reviewed September 21, 2026

When a repair makes sense, and when it doesn't

Artificial turf repair covers seam repair, turf wrinkles, lifted edges, a burn or melt patch, flattened turf in a traffic lane, a drainage fix, and pet damage near a gate or a dig spot. A repair is the right call when the problem is local: one seam open along a few feet, a corner that lifted after a storm, a scorch mark under a west-facing window. The rest of the lawn is doing its job, so there's no reason to replace it. We also repair turf other companies installed, which is most of what we see; the original crew doesn't have to still be in business, or even identifiable, for a seam to get fixed.

It's not worth patching when the turf is twelve to fifteen years old and showing wear everywhere, not only at the trouble spot, because new turf never quite matches sun-faded fiber, and paying repair labor toward a lawn that needs to come out soon anyway is money spent twice. The other sign it's time to stop patching: the same spot failing a second or third time, which usually means the base underneath is the real problem and no amount of reseaming fixes that. Turf replacement covers what that decision looks like.

How do you fix wrinkles, open seams and flattened turf?

Wrinkles come from a base that shifted or turf that was never stretched tight, and the fix is to lift the panel, pull it drum-tight, and re-secure the edge, not to weigh the bump down. Open seams are cut back to a clean stitch row and rejoined with seam tape and adhesive. Flattened turf is brushed hard against the grain; if the backing itself has crushed, that section gets replaced rather than just brushed.

Common turf problems, likely cause and the fix
SymptomUsual causeTypical fix
Wrinkle or wave in the middle of a panelBase shifted, or the turf was never stretched drum-tight during the original installLift, re-stretch, re-secure the edge; no iron or weight, that only hides it for a season
Open or separating seamAdhesive skinned before it bonded, often from gluing over a damp or dusty baseCut back to a clean stitch row, reseam with tape and adhesive under dry conditions
Lifted or curling edgeNails pulled loose, or wind got under an edge that wasn't anchored tightlyRe-nail into solid base at tighter spacing, or switch to an adhesive edge where nails keep failing
Burn or melt patchReflected sun off a low-E window; turf's polyethylene softens around 175–200°FCut out the affected section and set a matched patch; the window itself may need a film or an awning
Flattened turf in a traffic laneFoot traffic packed the blades down and pressed the infill flatPower broom against the grain; replace the section if the backing itself is crushed, not just the fiber
Water standing after rainThe base settled or never had enough slope; not a turf-drainage problemLift the area, add and recompact base to restore the 1–2% grade away from the house
Torn seam or urine-burned patch near a gateDigging at an open seam, or acidic urine pooling in one repeated spotReseam or patch the section; for recurring odor, a cleaning visit with an enzyme treatment usually handles the rest

How a repair visit actually goes

Here's the sequence on a typical call, whether it's a small patch or a wider re-stretch.

  1. You send photos or we come look. A phone photo of a wrinkle or an open seam is usually enough to quote a range before anyone's on site.
  2. We find the cause, not just the symptom. Lifting a corner shows whether the base underneath is still solid or whether it's soft, washed out or root-heaved.
  3. We cut to a clean edge. Patches and reseams are trimmed back to a stitch row on all sides so the tape has a straight line to bond to, not a ragged cut.
  4. Grain runs the same direction. Replacement turf, even from the same product line, gets checked against the existing pile direction before it's seamed in.
  5. Seams cure under weight. Sandbags or boards hold a fresh seam flat while the adhesive sets, usually a few hours depending on temperature and humidity.
  6. Infill goes back and we walk the perimeter. We top up infill over the repair and check the rest of the edge, since one storm-lifted corner is often not the only one.

What artificial turf repair costs

Artificial turf repair is priced by scope, not by the square footage of the whole lawn, and we haven't found a published Central Florida-specific price survey for it as of September 2026. What is published, from national installer cost guides, gives a reasonable frame: a small seam re-glue or patch under 20 sq ft runs roughly $350 to $950, a larger patch with matched turf and a full infill refresh runs $850 to $2,400, and a full re-stretch and re-nail on a lawn lifting across a wide area runs $1,800 to $5,500 (a 2026 repair-versus-replace cost breakdown). A single-issue service call in most U.S. markets lands around $500 to $1,000 for a few hours of labor and materials (a Los Angeles repair cost guide).

Those are market ranges, not our quote. Repairs here carry a minimum service charge, because a truck, tools and scrap turf show up whether the fix takes twenty minutes or two hours. Send photos first and we'll tell you which tier it's likely to land in before scheduling a visit.

Why Florida turf fails the way it does

Heat does most of the damage that ends up as a repair call. Full summer sun pushes turf past 150°F at the surface and can pass 160°F (installer heat measurements), and the expansion and contraction through that swing is what pulls a marginal seam apart over a year or two; a reflected hot spot off a west-facing window can push a small area past the point where the blades soften and melt. This post goes deeper on the window-glare problem specifically.

Storm season adds the other half: wind gets under an edge that wasn't anchored tightly, and heavy rain finds any low spot where the sandy base has settled, common on Kissimmee's fine, loose native soil after a few wet seasons. Live oak roots are the quieter cause, lifting a seam from below over a year or two as a root grows under turf laid too close to the trunk. None of this is a defect in the turf material; it's a base or edge problem that shows up as a turf problem.

Does a repair need a permit or HOA sign-off?

Almost never. A repair restores what was already there rather than changing the footprint or the material, so it doesn't typically trigger the review a first-time installation would. The exception is a repair that also changes something visible from the street, such as re-anchoring an edge with a different border material; in a community with strict guidelines, mention that change when you tell the board the lawn is being worked on. What a Florida HOA can and can not restrict explains where that line sits, and the state standard requiring anchored edges and seams on a new install (Rule 62-308.100) is a reasonable bar for judging whether a repair was done right.

What a bad repair looks like next season

A patch that doesn't match is the most obvious failure: a different lot, a different sun exposure, or a different manufacturer's green shows up as a visible rectangle for years, because turf doesn't blend the way a lawn does. Less obvious until it fails again: a seam reglued over a base that was never cleaned or dried, which looks fine on install day and opens again within a season because the adhesive skinned before it bonded.

Nails driven back into the holes they pulled out of don't hold any better the second time. And a wrinkle that gets ironed flat or weighted down instead of re-stretched will be back by the next hot week, because the extra material is still there, just hidden instead of removed.

After the repair

Keep foot traffic light on a fresh seam for about a day while the adhesive fully cures. Brush the repaired section against the grain once it's set so it blends with the surrounding pile, then give it a hose rinse to settle the new infill. Walk the yard after the next named storm the way you would any other time; a repair holds up to the same wind and rain as the rest of the lawn, no better and no worse. If the same spot fails twice, that's the signal to ask about the base rather than request a third patch. This guide covers when a storm-related repair might be a claim instead of an out-of-pocket fix.

Who is the best turf repair contractor near me?

Ask that question with a follow-up: will they explain why the problem happened, not just what they'll do to hide it? A contractor worth hiring lifts the damaged area, shows you the base, and tells you whether the cause is fixed or just covered. Ask whether they'll repair turf they didn't install, since a surprising number of companies won't touch another crew's work, and ask for the minimum charge up front so a twenty-minute fix doesn't turn into a surprise invoice.

Send photos of the seam, wrinkle or spot and we'll tell you what tier it's likely in before we schedule a visit.

Questions people ask

Can a wrinkle be fixed without replacing the whole lawn?

Yes, in almost every case. The panel is lifted, re-stretched drum-tight and re-secured at the edge. Replacing the whole lawn over a wrinkle is rarely necessary unless the same panel has wrinkled more than once, which usually points to a base problem instead of a stretching problem.

Why did a seam open only two or three years after installation?

Most early seam failures trace back to adhesive applied over a base that was damp, dusty or not fully cured, which lets the bond look fine on install day and let go later. Foot traffic across a fresh seam before the adhesive sets can cause the same result.

Can you match a repair patch to turf that's faded from years of sun?

Not perfectly. New turf is always a shade greener than several summers of UV exposure have left the surrounding lawn, so a patch on an older lawn stays visible, at least for a while. It solves the functional problem even where it doesn't disappear visually.

Is a lifted turf edge after a storm urgent?

Worth addressing within a week or two. Wind and rain both work under a lifted corner and can widen the problem, and standing water at a lifted seam breaks down the adhesive faster than a dry edge would.

Will you repair turf that another company installed?

Yes. Most repair calls we get are on lawns we didn't originally build. What matters is whether the base underneath is sound enough to repair; if it isn't, we'll say so instead of patching over it.

What's the smallest repair job you'll take?

A single seam or a patch under a few square feet, though it still carries the minimum service charge that covers the trip and setup. Text a photo and we'll tell you what to expect before booking a visit.

How long does a typical repair visit take?

A single seam or small patch is usually a two- to four-hour visit including cure time under weight. A full re-stretch of a lifting panel, or a repair that needs a discontinued turf matched, can take a full day.
